This study examines the behavior of the Cohen-Macaulay property and related attributes, such as Gorenstein and complete intersection properties, under specific ring extensions. We introduce a novel class of complete intersection rings, defined as rings that are intersections of finitely many prime ideals, each with a residue of codimension two. We establish that the intersection of any finite collection of complete intersection rings remains a complete intersection ring. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain ring extensions preserve the Cohen-Macaulay property even when the original ring is not Gorenstein. We also provide an explicit characterization of the conditions under which the extension $R \subset R[x]$ results in $R[x]$ being a complete intersection over $R$.

The magnetic and transport properties of the multiferroic compound Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ were examined under high pressure up to 10 GPa using a piston-cylinder device. The study reveals that the magnetic ordering temperature, $T_{\rm N}$, decreases with pressure at low values, but this suppression ceases above 4 GPa. At low temperatures, the magnetic ordering transitions from a spiral to a canted antiferromagnetic state, a shift driven by the suppression of the spiral component. The magnetic susceptibility, $\chi$, exhibits a broad maximum at $T_{\rm m}$, which shifts to higher temperatures as pressure increases. The magnetic susceptibility data are modeled using the modified Curie-Weiss law, yielding a Curie temperature $T_{\rm C}$ that rises with pressure. The observed pressure-induced suppression of the spiral component is attributed to the compression of the Fe-O-Fe bond angle.

This study examines the distribution of trading benchmarks within the financial sector, revealing a pronounced tendency toward fat tails. We propose a novel approach to forecast the probability of extreme occurrences, incorporating the influence of both volatility and trading volume. Our methodology is evaluated using data from the S&P 500 index, the CAC 40 index, and the DAX 40 index.

We introduce a tunable on-resonance and off-resonance add-drop filter based on a double-disk cavity optomechanical system. This design achieves a maximum drop efficiency of 99.8% and supports a 20% tunability range. Furthermore, the filter exhibits a high extinction ratio of 40 dB for non-resonant light. We anticipate that this configuration will be valuable for various applications, including multiplexing and demultiplexing, as well as optical routing.

The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly reshaped daily life, with online user activity serving as a vital indicator for evaluating the effectiveness of public health measures. This study introduces a framework for analyzing Twitter data to assess the impact of such interventions. By employing a novel approach to model temporal trends in online activity, the method quantifies the deviation of observed counts from expected levels. This framework was applied to examine the effects of COVID-19 lockdowns in the United States and the United Kingdom. The findings reveal that while online activity in both nations closely matched pre-intervention trends during the initial phases, the trajectories diverged significantly in subsequent weeks. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that Twitter data can effectively detect alterations in online behavior resulting from public health policies.

This study introduces a new image compression method utilizing deep neural networks, which employs a distinct approach to achieving high throughput rates. The proposed method utilizes a hybrid architecture combining a convolutional autoencoder with a set of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) designed to generate multiple bitstreams. This strategy enables the system to meet the necessary high-speed throughput requirements for numerous practical compression applications. The research demonstrates that the method can deliver compression ratios ranging from 1:1 to 1:128, all while maintaining image quality at PSNR levels of 30 dB or higher.

This study reports the first observation of the decay process $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$, utilizing data from $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 10.52 GeV. The analysis leverages a dataset of 1.06 $\times$ 10$^{9}$ $B\bar{B}$ pairs collected by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII facility. The branching fraction for this decay is determined to be $(1.00 \pm 0.12 \pm 0.06) \times 10^{-6}$, where the first uncertainty represents statistical error and the second reflects systematic uncertainty. Furthermore, the differential decay distributions are analyzed across various $D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ invariant mass intervals.

Optimal transport (OT) loss functions are increasingly prevalent in machine learning, particularly for tasks like generative modeling and domain adaptation. However, their performance is often compromised by outliers, which can drastically skew OT estimates. This study examines the impact of outliers on OT losses within machine learning contexts. We demonstrate that the OT loss is highly sensitive to outliers, causing a significant loss of robustness. To address this, we introduce a novel robust OT loss that mitigates outlier effects, proving that it maintains consistency with the true OT loss as sample sizes grow. Furthermore, we establish a finite-sample bound for the discrepancy between our robust estimator and the standard OT loss, showing that the robust version achieves $O(\sqrt{n})$ convergence in probability, whereas the standard version degrades to $O(n)$ under contamination. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both generative modeling and domain adaptation, confirming the resilience of our approach against out-of-distribution data.

Collaborative AI agents capable of partnering with humans in games like Hanabi are essential for advancing human-AI collaboration. Although recent advancements have produced agents that excel at solving Hanabi puzzles, they often fail to display cooperative behaviors that align with human expectations. This paper introduces a novel framework for training agents to exhibit human-like cooperation in both games and tasks. We introduce "Q-learning with a human prior," a method that trains agents to demonstrate human-consistent behavior even in unfamiliar situations. Furthermore, we present "Q-learning with human feedback," a framework that integrates human feedback into the learning process to refine agent policies. Our experiments demonstrate that these agents surpass existing methods in generating human-consistent behavior across diverse cooperative scenarios.

Supersymmetry (SUSY) is a framework where every particle possesses a partner with altered spin. In the context of the Standard Model, the Higgs boson's mass is prone to large quantum corrections that would push its value far beyond the observed 125 GeV. However, if supersymmetry holds true at the TeV scale, these corrections are significantly mitigated, allowing the Higgs mass to remain near 125 GeV. This study investigates the implications of SUSY for the relic abundance of dark matter, specifically focusing on a scenario where the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) is a stable, massive neutralino. We examine a minimal SUSY extension of the Standard Model featuring a single neutralino LSP, the lightest chargino, and the lightest stop quark. Assuming the lightest chargino and stop are degenerate in mass, the annihilation process into top quarks is enhanced, reducing the neutralino relic density. We identify the parameter space where dark matter mass is sufficiently small to satisfy observational constraints while remaining consistent with LHC limits on chargino and stop masses.

The growing prevalence of intricate visual representations, such as network graphs, necessitates a deeper understanding of how individuals from diverse backgrounds interact with them. This study investigates the influence of complex visualization formats on users' cognitive performance and task performance across three distinct occupations: data scientists, software developers, and data engineers. The research examines two specific cognitive skills: spatial ability and working memory capacity. The findings indicate that spatial ability plays a more significant role in task performance for data scientists, whereas working memory capacity is more influential for software developers and data engineers. Additionally, the study explores how different visualization types affect these metrics, revealing that node-link based visualizations generally yield superior task performance compared to both graph-based and matrix-based representations.

This paper examines the connection between cycle-based redundancy and first-order inductive proof methods, specifically $ \mathbb{Q}_1^- $ induction, within the context of automated theorem proving. It demonstrates that any clause set cycle can be derived using $ \mathbb{Q}_1^- $ induction, with the exception of cyclicities linked to the Pigeonhole Principle. Furthermore, the authors present a theorem proving the converse regarding polynomial cycle systems: if such a system is derivable via $ \mathbb{Q}_1^- $ induction, it is also derivable through cycle-based reasoning.

This study investigates neural network methods for retrieving graphs, specifically focusing on a multi-task learning framework that leverages auxiliary tasks to enhance performance on the primary objective. The research evaluates the impact of various graph neural networks and neural text encoders, along with different fusion strategies, on the main task of graph retrieval. The dataset consists of pairs comprising a query graph and a context-rich document containing an embedded target graph, with the aim of identifying the most relevant query graph based on textual cues. The paper introduces and analyzes a multi-task learning approach that utilizes supplementary tasks to boost the primary graph retrieval performance.

Recent computer vision advancements have predominantly relied on large-scale, manually annotated datasets. In contrast, this work introduces a novel approach to enhance computer vision by leveraging the rich textual annotations associated with images. By utilizing Natural Language Processing techniques, we can generate pseudo-labels from these captions to refine computer vision algorithms. Our method employs a two-stage process: first, we use a pre-trained language model to predict object attributes and their relationships within an image, then we apply these inferred labels to train a computer vision model. We tested this approach on the ImageNet dataset, demonstrating that it yields competitive performance compared to models trained using only ground truth labels.

Load shedding, a common occurrence in developing nations, severely impacts households by curtailing electricity access. This issue is particularly acute for homes with higher energy demands, such as those with air conditioning, where power outages can lead to a dramatic rise in indoor temperatures. To mitigate this, we introduce a system designed to manage indoor thermal conditions during load shedding events. By leveraging a model predictive control (MPC) framework, the system anticipates temperature shifts caused by specific load shedding schedules and proactively adjusts the thermostat accordingly. This proactive regulation minimizes the total energy consumption required to keep indoor temperatures within a predefined comfort range. We validate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations using the TROPICS model, which captures the thermal dynamics of a residential building.

Event coreference resolution (ECR) involves identifying all references tied to the same event within a text. A primary challenge in this task is the frequent co-occurrence of multiple instances of the same event within a single document, which leads to incorrect associations. This issue is particularly prevalent in dense domains like biomedicine. To address this, we introduce a new dataset comprising event coreference annotations for 1,000 PubMed articles. The dataset includes event mentions alongside their contextual information and entity links. We evaluated our benchmark against the state-of-the-art ECR system, Doc2Vec, demonstrating its limitations in medical texts. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new neural network-based model that leverages the contextual embeddings of event mentions to generate dense representations. Our method utilizes a novel attention mechanism to weigh the contextual embeddings of mentions, thereby improving the accuracy of coreference link prediction. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms Doc2Vec, achieving a 10.2% improvement in F1 score.

The Complementarity Knapsack Problem (CKP) is a significant extension of the standard 0/1 knapsack problem characterized by additional constraints that enforce complementarity among selected items. This paper introduces a new branch-and-bound algorithm designed to solve the CKP, which utilizes a specialized relaxation technique to generate upper bounds. This approach is particularly effective for NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, where traditional methods often struggle with scalability. By leveraging the newly developed upper bounds, the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing solutions in the literature. Furthermore, computational experiments on randomly generated instances with up to 100 variables demonstrate that the algorithm can efficiently solve problems with 50 variables in under 10 seconds and handle instances with 100 variables in under one minute.

This paper investigates a broad category of left skew derivations denoted as $F$, referred to specifically as a generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivation on a semiprime ring $R$. Under the condition that the sum $m-d$ is not identically zero for a fixed element $d \in \mathbb{N}$, it is established that any such derivation $F$ corresponds to the form $F(x) = a d(x) + g(x) n$ for some $a,b \in U(R)$, where $n$ represents centralizer of $R$ and $n d$ denotes a Jordan derivation on $R$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that if $n$ is a generalized $(m,n)$ Jordan derivation on $R$ and $n(d) = 0$ for all elements $n$ in $R$, then $n d$ is indeed a Jordan derivation on $R$.

We introduce a systematic method for factoring the low- and high-energy components of scattering amplitudes within effective field theories. This approach is applicable to any amplitude derived from an effective Lagrangian, encompassing both tree-level and loop-generated terms. We provide a comprehensive derivation of the factorization formula for tree-level amplitudes and apply it to examine the low-energy behavior of the leading-order chiral Lagrangian. Furthermore, we demonstrate how factorization extends to the leading-order quantum corrections arising from the chiral Lagangian.

We investigate the decay rates of the "rough set" variant of Favard length for nonlinear settings, demonstrating that the decay rates previously established by Bourgain, Guth, and Zorin in the context of the Strange Inequality also apply to this specific class of Favard length.

This paper introduces a new Robust Tube approach for Model Predictive Control (MPC) designed to enhance the control of systems subject to disturbances. The proposed method integrates the advantages of both the standard Robust Tube MPC and the Receding Horizon Robust Control (RHRC) techniques. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this variant ensures the system's state remains within a predictable region over time, while computational demands are significantly lower than those of RHRC. The effectiveness of the new algorithm is validated through numerical simulations on a two-link robotic manipulator.

The field-induced anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a topic of significant interest in both theoretical and experimental physics. While the first-order field-dependent curvature has been extensively researched, the second-order is often overlooked. This work introduces a unified framework to examine the AHE arising from second-order field-dependent curvature, specifically within the context of Weyl fermions. We demonstrate that the second-order curvature can be expressed via a Witten index, which is determined by the topological invariants of the underlying Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we establish that the second-order field-dependent curvature is intrinsically linked to the first-order curvature, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of the conditions under which it vanishes. Finally, we discuss the potential experimental verification of this phenomenon.

Analyzing call graphs is a critical step in optimizing large-scale parallel applications. This paper introduces a novel method for generating Sankey visualizations of call graphs, specifically designed to address the complexity of massive parallel systems. By employing a multi-pass algorithm, the proposed technique aggregates data across multiple views to create an "ensemble-Sankey" visualization. This approach effectively highlights the most frequently occurring execution paths while filtering out noise caused by infrequent or outlier paths. The method is demonstrated through a case study of a large-scale parallel simulation, where it successfully identifies key execution paths that were missed by traditional single-pass Sankey visualizations. Additionally, the study examines the algorithm's scalability and its performance when processing highly complex call graphs.

Pre-training language models (LMs) on extensive text corpora has proven to be an effective strategy for generating high-quality representations. However, these models often struggle with downstream tasks when the data they encounter differs from their training distribution, a problem that intensifies when training corpora evolve over time. This paper investigates the impact of temporal shifts on the Wikipedia news graph, a dataset constructed from English Wikipedia articles. We analyze how temporal distributional shifts affect the performance of LMs on news classification tasks, specifically examining the role of temporal data splitting and the use of temporal data augmentation. Our findings indicate that temporal shifts within the Wikipedia news graph pose significant challenges for LM performance on news classification, and we demonstrate that temporal data augmentation serves as an effective solution to mitigate this issue.

Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) are frequently observed in solar flares, yet their underlying physical mechanisms remain unclear. This study examines the temporal evolution of QPPs in solar flares by analyzing simultaneous observations from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) and the High-Resolution Telescope (HRT) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The analysis focuses on a flare occurring on 2017 June 1, which exhibited QPPs in both AIA's 171 Å and 2500 Å channels. The observed oscillations were localized to the flare ribbons and coronal loops extending from them. The AIA 171 Å channel captured QPPs with a period of approximately 120 seconds, while the 2500 Å channel revealed a longer period of roughly 250 seconds. The study concludes that these QPPs are driven by the rapid expansion of the flare ribbons, which compresses the coronal loops. The observed periods correspond to the fundamental mode of the loops, which are modulated by the acceleration of the ribbons. The acceleration is attributed to the rapid expansion of the flare ribbons, which compresses the coronal loops. This study introduces a novel approach for identifying anomalies in images by employing a supervised learning framework. The proposed method utilizes a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) to reconstruct images from a training set, isolating anomalies by calculating a specific metric for each data point. To achieve this, we implemented the cGAN architecture and introduced a new variant called the Conditional Patch-GAN. The effectiveness of the anomaly detection system was evaluated using a dataset of synthetic images containing defects. The findings demonstrate that the introduced method yields superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper investigates the Cauchy problem associated with dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I equations in $\mathbb{R}^2$, defined by the operator parameter $\delta$ ($0<\delta\leq 1$). Strong dispersion conditions ($\delta\geq\frac{2}{3}$) are established as necessary for well-posedness in the critical Sobolev space $H^s(\mathbb{R}^2)$ for $s>\frac{3}{8}$. Additionally, the global well-posedness of the equation in dimensions where strong dispersion holds ($\delta\geq\frac{2}{3}$) within the critical Sobolev space $H^{1/8+\epsilon(\delta)}\times\mathbb{R}^2$ is proven. For the subcritical range ($\frac{3}{8}\geq\delta>\frac{1}{2}$), the specific threshold $s=\frac{3}{8+\delta}$ is identified as sufficient for global well-posedness, while the remaining intermediate case ($s\leq\frac{1}{2}$) is addressed.

Kramers' theorem guarantees that fermionic systems with an odd number of fermions possess doubly degenerate energy levels. This paper introduces a method to derive fermionic correlation functions from bosonic ones, enabling the extension of Kramers' theorem to $n$-point functions. We demonstrate that fermionic correlation functions defined on a closed manifold vanish whenever an odd number of external legs are present. This result is further generalized to systems exhibiting fermionic parity symmetry. Finally, we apply these generalized fermionic-Wick theorems to $n$-point functions within $c=1$ superconformal Liouville theory.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning-driven channel forecasting framework designed for millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive MIMO systems, specifically addressing high-speed vehicular environments. The framework leverages a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to predict future channel states by integrating historical channel data with vehicle dynamics. The proposed method is validated using a stochastic channel model that accounts for both high-speed movement and mmWave propagation characteristics. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional channel prediction techniques.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework for inferring income inequality at the microregional level, utilizing small-area data from the Italian Labour Force Survey (LFS). The approach integrates a Bayesian log-normal distribution with a mixed linear regression model to generate area-specific estimates of income inequality. The analysis relies on the hierarchical structure of the LFS, which provides sufficient data to estimate the model's parameters. The proposed method is validated through a simulation study, and subsequently, it is applied to derive microregional inequality measures within the metropolitan area of Milan.

This study addresses the Szeg\o{} projector for the small-scale eigenvalues of the Grauert tube associated with any compact manifold featuring positive Yamabe constant. By employing a technique rooted in the meromorphic extension of boundary values of harmonic functions, we establish that this projector is expressed as a finite sum involving powers of the Szeg\o{}-Beltrami operator.

This study presents MARINLINGA, a novel algorithm designed to calculate reverse Line graphs. MARINLINGA is an adaptation of the widely used KASSELINGA, which was originally designed for reversing the Max-Clique algorithm. While the latter operates in $O(n^2)$ time complexity, MARINLINGA achieves a worst-case complexity of $O(mn)$, where $n$ represents the number of vertices and $m$ represents the number of edges in the input graph. This paper demonstrates that for acyclic quivers, associated roots of non-self-intersecting curves correspond to real Schur roots. Furthermore, it demonstrates that when restricted to the case of acyclic quivers, the two proposed proofs yield identical outcomes.

Software applications often rely on numerous libraries, which can lead to bloat and hinder maintainability. This study examines the impact of such bloated dependencies on software quality within the R programming language. We conducted an analysis of 1,000 R packages from the CRAN repository, focusing on library usage patterns. Our results indicate that package authors frequently include unnecessary libraries, and this inclusion tends to increase as package size grows. Furthermore, we observe that these superfluous dependencies are rarely utilized within the package's own code. To address this, we developed a static analysis tool designed to identify unnecessary dependencies, which demonstrates high precision. Utilizing this tool, we propose a set of guidelines to mitigate dependency bloat.

We investigate a model of "abstract polymer chains" where chains of length $N$ are constructed from a sequence of $N$ symbols drawn from an alphabet of size $M$. In this framework, the "degree of kinship" between two chains is determined by the proportion of matching symbols at corresponding positions. We examine the statistical distribution of this overlap across all possible pairs of chains and analyze the model's properties using a continuous, stochastic approximation. Our analysis reveals that the system's dynamics can be described by a Fokker-Planck equation, where the polymer sequences behave analogously to a system of Brownian particles. We further explore the model's implications for understanding the evolutionary relationships among species.

This paper investigates multistage distributionally robust optimization (DRO) by focusing on the specific scenario paths that matter most. We introduce a method to formulate these paths as constraints within the DRO framework, enabling the selection of specific paths based on the decision maker's prior knowledge. To address the computational challenges posed by this approach, we develop a column generation algorithm that solves the master problem via a specialized Lagrangian relaxation. We propose a Lagrangian subproblem that can be resolved using a scenario reduction technique, alongside a specialized procedure to handle the master problem. We also establish convergence guarantees for the proposed method and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments.

This paper introduces a novel approach for predicting future video characteristics and action outcomes by leveraging a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to forecast future features and an Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to determine actions. The system utilizes an RNN to model the temporal evolution of video attributes and employs a CNN to forecast outcomes based on those features. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through its ability to handle both short- and long-term action anticipation tasks.

We examine the emergence of deep thermalization within quantum many-body systems, defined as a state where local subsystems reach thermal equilibrium characterized by low temperature and minimal entropy. This phenomenon is investigated in two distinct frameworks: first, in isolated systems driven by unitary time evolution from an initial state, and second, in interacting integrable models coupled to non-integrable environments via open quantum dynamics. Our analysis demonstrates that both scenarios exhibit thermalization toward temperatures approaching absolute zero. These findings are substantiated by numerical calculations on representative models, specifically the transverse-field Ising model and the one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model.

This paper investigates the properties of pseudo-differential operators defined on homogeneous trees. We establish boundedness criteria for such operators, characterized by specific conditions on both the symbol and the underlying measure space. Furthermore, we examine the compactness of these operators, as well as the associated questions of composition and trace.

The rapid expansion of 5G networks has sparked significant public concern regarding the potential health impacts of radiofrequency radiation. This study examines the electromagnetic exposure faced by smartphone users in 5G environments, contrasting it with exposure levels from earlier generations of cellular technology. The analysis evaluates exposure from both cellular radio base stations and the smartphone itself acting as a mobile phone. Results indicate that overall exposure to electromagnetic fields from 5G networks is substantially lower than that experienced in 4G networks.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are prone to producing overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, a behavior that poses significant risks in safety-critical applications. While recent approaches have attempted to mitigate this issue by incorporating OOD detection capabilities (OODs) into the model, these methods often incur substantial computational costs and require retraining. This paper introduces Class-OD Detection Embeddings (CODEs), an efficient framework designed to simultaneously detect class predictions and OOD samples. CODEs are generated by training a classifier to distinguish between in-distribution and OOD feature representations. The approach is straightforward to implement, computationally efficient, and does not require retraining the base DNN. Experiments demonstrate that CODEs achieve superior OOD detection performance compared to existing methods while maintaining high accuracy on in-distribution classification tasks.

This study examines the azimuthal jet correlation sensitivity within the 13 TeV proton-proton environment, utilizing the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on the correlation between a leading trigger jet and a subleading associated jet, employing the $\Delta\phi$ distribution and the $R_{\phi\phi}$ metric. Measurements are conducted across various leading jet transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}^{\rm jet}$) ranges, spanning from 20 to 120 GeV, with associated jet $p_{\rm T}$ limits between 20 and 40 GeV. The observed data are compared against theoretical predictions generated using Monte Carlo event generators. Furthermore, the study evaluates the influence of underlying event and multi-jet background subtraction methodologies on the resulting measurements.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in numerous domains, including image classification, object detection, and speech recognition. However, these advancements have come at the cost of requiring vast amounts of labeled data. To address this limitation, this study introduces a novel semi-supervised and unsupervised deep learning framework designed to enhance model performance by utilizing unlabeled data. The methodology involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on unlabeled data, followed by the generation of synthetic samples that are subsequently used to train a support vector machine (SVM). Experimental results demonstrate that this semi-supervised approach outperforms traditional supervised learning methods.

This study introduces a novel approach to outlier detection that leverages the reconstruction error of an autoencoder. By training the autoencoder on a dataset of normal samples, the method identifies anomalies based on their elevated reconstruction error compared to normal instances. Experiments conducted on the MNIST and CIFAR10 image datasets demonstrate that this technique surpasses the performance of several state-of-the-art methods.

This work investigates the non-linear equation $u(t) + \mathcal{A}u(t) + \mathcal{M}(t, u(t)) = f(t)$ defined on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ denotes a maximal monotone operator, $\mathcal{M}$ is a mapping characterized by monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity, and $u \in C^1((0, T)\times \mathcal{H})$ represents a classical solution. We establish that for every $t \in (0, T]$, a unique mild solution exists and remains classical under the condition that $f$ is a bounded continuous function. Furthermore, we derive an $L^2$-estimate for the time derivative of the mild solution.

We examine the production of photons from the decay of neutrinos produced in cosmic ray interactions within the atmosphere. This process is enhanced by light (pseudo)scalar mediators that connect the Standard Model's lepton doublet to the Standard Model Higgs boson. We demonstrate that current data from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array can constrain the parameters of these mediators, and we show that upcoming observations could uncover a new physics signal. Furthermore, we indicate that existing and future neutrino telescopes can also probe this scenario.

The brain's intricate architecture and function are defined by the complex interplay between neurons and glia. In this study, we examine how the activity of glia influences neural network behavior. We introduce a model where excitatory neurons connect via synapses, while inhibitory neurons form a web of connections with one another. We demonstrate that this system naturally exhibits a glial activity state that responds to the input of excitatory neurons. By integrating this dynamic into a rate model, we can effectively simulate the behavior of the full network. We apply this approach to investigate the emergence of oscillations and the synchronization of excitatory neurons. Our findings reveal that the system displays diverse synchronization states, including incoherence, phase locking, and amplitude locking. We also show that the dynamics of excitatory neurons are significantly shaped by the inhibitory network's activity. Furthermore, we establish that the transition from amplitude locking to incoherence occurs via a subcritical Hopf bifurcation, a process that generates hysteresis.

This study investigates how a neutral spin-1/2 particle behaves when passing through a double-slit barrier within a magnetic vortex field, utilizing the Dirac equation with an explicit magnetic monopole term. The findings indicate that, in addition to the standard double-slit interference pattern, an interference effect arises specifically from the neutral particle's coupling to the magnetic vortex field.

This study examines the first-passage time distribution for the nth hitting event of a Brownian particle encountering a moving boundary. We demonstrate that, for large times, the probability of reaching the boundary for the nth time scales as $t^{-3/2}$.

We demonstrate that for any knot $K$ which is an $L$-space knot, the associated formal semi-group derived from its Alexander polynomial encodes the knot's knot Floer homology. Furthermore, we investigate formal semi-groups for the connected sums of L-space knots and propose a conjecture regarding the conditions under which the formal semi-group of a connected sum can be derived from the sum of the summands' individual semi-groups.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-dimensional, incompressible fluid with constant density, initially defined by the Navier-Stokes equations. It is proven that, given initial data with a finite $H^3$ norm, the solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations converge to those of the 2D Euler equations in a way that preserves this $H^3$ bound. This result holds for any initial data within $H^s$ where $s > 2$ that is close to a specific 2D Euler solution possessing regularity $s > 2$.

This study introduces an ensemble deep-learning approach designed to enhance object detection performance. The proposed framework integrates multiple distinct object detectors, each trained on different subsets of the data, to boost overall accuracy. The core methodology relies on a fusion of the individual outputs generated by these detectors. Experimental results demonstrate that this ensemble technique achieves superior results compared to a single detector, particularly when applied to the object detection task on the PASCAL VOC benchmark.

Identifier names serve as fundamental building blocks in software, yet their specific characteristics are often unclear. This study investigates the naming conventions of various identifiers in Java, including classes, methods, and attributes, by analyzing a dataset of 1,000 classes sourced from the DroidBench. The analysis reveals consistent naming patterns for each identifier type, with certain forms appearing significantly more frequently than others. Additionally, the research highlights that these naming patterns are strongly influenced by the semantic roles of the identifiers.

Consider the unital associative algebra generated by the symbols $e_{ij}$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$, subject to the relations $e_{ij}e_{kl} = \delta_{j,k} e_{i,l}$ and $e_{ij}e_{kl} = 0$ when $j \neq k$. A vector formed by a linear combination of these generators is termed a **NIL vector** if it annihilates the entire algebra. This study focuses on identifying all such vectors. The central result establishes that a linear combination $\sum_{i,j=1}^n \alpha_{ij} e_{ij}$ constitutes a NIL vector if and only if there exist $n$ linearly independent vectors $u_1, \dots, u_n$ in an $n$-dimensional vector space such that $\alpha_{ij} = \lambda_i u_i(u_j)$ for all $i,j$, where $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ are $n$ mutually distinct scalars.

The study employs a phase-field model to simulate the grain growth of duplex and triplex microstructures, where the latter consists of two distinct phases. By analyzing the evolution of the phase-field equation, the authors demonstrate that, during isotropic grain growth, the phase with the lower interfacial energy dictates the overall kinetics. Furthermore, the model incorporates a novel mechanism to simulate the precipitation of a second phase within existing grains, enabling the formation of triplex microstructures. These findings are corroborated by numerical results, which also reveal that the morphology of a triplex microstructure is defined by the interfacial energies of the three phases involved.

Accurately estimating 3D human pose and shape from monocular images is essential for numerous applications, including augmented reality, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant advancements in this field, current models still struggle with generalization, particularly when encountering unseen subjects or complex body configurations. This paper introduces a novel approach that enhances generalization by leveraging a comprehensive dataset of diverse body types and postures. We utilize this data to train a generative model capable of producing realistic 3D human shapes and poses. This generated data serves as a critical augmentation strategy for training a 3D estimation network, thereby improving its ability to handle previously unseen cases. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions on challenging benchmarks involving previously unseen individuals and extreme poses.

We introduce a theoretical framework for superconductivity in dilute electron systems featuring strong correlations, specifically those with negative $U$-centers. This model, which incorporates a lattice of $d$-electrons and a background of $s$-electrons, is derived from the first-principles density functional theory (DFT) and is validated by its ability to reproduce the electronic band structure of the material $\mathrm{ZrTe}_5$. Within this model, $d$-electrons form a Mott insulator, while $s$-electrons constitute a superconducting background. The interaction between these two systems yields a superconducting instability characterized by a critical temperature that scales with the density of states at the Fermi level. Consequently, this approach offers a pathway to explain the observed high-temperature superconductivity in $\mathrm{ZrTe}_5$.

Scalar leptoquarks represent a compelling class of new physics, having been proposed to address various anomalies in high-energy experiments. This study examines the implications of a complex, triplet scalar leptoquantum field, which possesses a distinct mass and vacuum expectation value. We investigate a model where this new triplet couples with the first generation of quarks and leptons, thereby explaining the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and addressing the proton decay limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed model remains viable by showing it satisfies current constraints from direct searches, the muon $g-2$ anomaly, proton decay limits, and the flavor sector.

Over the last few years, machine learning has become an integral part of numerous fields, including natural language processing, computer vision, and data mining. In this context, category theory has emerged as a powerful tool for abstractly modeling computational processes and facilitating the integration of various machine learning algorithms. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in applying category theory to machine learning, highlighting significant developments from 2018 to 2021. Furthermore, we examine how category theory has been utilized in recent years to address diverse machine learning applications, ranging from natural language processing and computer vision to data mining.

This study addresses the terminal sliding mode control (TSMC) problem for Newton's motion dynamics of second-order systems. A primary challenge with TSMC is that the resulting sliding mode surface and control law can induce the "singularity issue," which degrades system performance. To address this, we propose a new TSMC strategy that avoids this issue. The approach first establishes a sliding mode surface that guarantees finite-time convergence. Subsequently, we introduce a control law that ensures the system states reach the sliding mode surface in finite time without triggering the singularity. The proposed method is validated through a simulation of a double inverted pendulum system. The results indicate that the suggested control scheme effectively achieves finite-time convergence while eliminating the singularity problem.

The rapid advancement of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) has created an urgent need for non-destructive methods to characterize their internal structures. While non-destructive imaging techniques like X-ray computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are well-established, they often fail to capture the intricate details of LIB internal architecture. In contrast, non-destructive spectroscopy, such as Raman spectroscopy, offers superior sensitivity to material composition and structural variations. This study introduces a novel, non-destructive approach that leverages Raman spectroscopy to quantify the internal architecture of lithium-ion batteries. The proposed method utilizes a deep learning framework to map Raman spectra to internal features, specifically the electrode's porosity and the distribution of lithium species. The framework's performance is validated using a custom-built experimental setup equipped with a 532 nm laser and a 60x objective lens. The results demonstrate that the model can accurately predict electrode porosity and the spatial distribution of lithium species with high precision.

This study introduces a discrete-time tracking control strategy for a gantry crane, designed to enhance operational safety and efficiency. The proposed approach leverages a nonlinear model derived from the system's kinematics and dynamics, utilizing the backstepping framework to synthesize the controller. By integrating the backstepping method with the Lyapunov stability theory, the research demonstrates that the control scheme guarantees the boundedness of all signals and ensures the tracking error converges to a compact set. The efficacy of this discrete-time approach is validated through numerical simulations, which further highlight its superior performance compared to traditional continuous-time control methods.

Image captioning systems have evolved significantly, achieving state-of-the-art performance on popular benchmarks like COCO. This success is largely driven by the availability of massive, automatically generated captioning datasets such as VCPAID CAPS, which offer vast quantities of diverse descriptions. However, these datasets suffer from inherent flaws, including low precision, poor diversity, and a bias toward common objects. To address these challenges, we introduce a new approach that leverages the rich semantic information within captions to refine both caption generation and evaluation. Our method employs a fine-grained evaluation model to assess caption quality and diversity, followed by the utilization of a reinforcement learning framework to optimize the generation process. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields superior performance across multiple metrics, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods.

A collection of strings $S$ is defined as well-connected if, for every pair of distinct strings $s_1, s_2 \in S$, there exists a string $s$ in $S$ (where $s \neq s_1$ and $s \neq s_2$) that shares a common prefix with both $s_1$ and $s_2$. This paper presents a linear-time algorithm capable of determining whether a given set of pairwise disjoint strings is well-connected.

Ehresmann semigroups are semigroups defined by an algebraic structure resembling that of partial semigroups alongside a partial order. Originally introduced by Peter M. Higgins in 1991, this concept has become a vital framework for analyzing partial functions. This paper outlines fundamental properties of ordered Ehresmann semigroups and introduces the specific structure of a free object within this category.

Self-attention architectures have become the standard for numerous NLP tasks, yet their theoretical underpinnings remain elusive. This paper investigates the computational complexity of Transformer networks by examining their depth-attention width trade-off. We demonstrate that for a specific class of functions, increasing the network's depth allows for a reduction in network width within the self-attention framework. Furthermore, we establish that a network of depth $d$ and width $w$ can be substituted by an equivalent network with depth $d+1$ and width $w-1$. These insights offer fresh perspectives on Transformer complexity and suggest a path toward more efficient model designs.

This study investigates the synthesis of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles (NPs) via a sol-gel method, utilizing the calcuration temperature as a variable to analyze their structural, morphological, and optical characteristics. The resulting NPs were evaluated for their photocatalytic efficiency in degrading methylene blue (MB) under UV light irradiation. NPs prepared at 160$^{\circ}$C exhibited superior performance compared to bulk BiFeO$_{3}$, achieving a degradation rate of 99.5% in 120 minutes. This enhancement is attributed to the formation of a heterojunction between BiFeO$_{3}$ and TiO$_{2}$, which facilitates the separation of electron-hole pairs. Additionally, the study examined the influence of varying BiFeO$_{3}$ concentrations on MB degradation, identifying an optimal concentration of 10 mg/L.

Reconstructing 3D objects held in hands from a single RGB image is a difficult task because the object's geometry is often obscured by the hand's occlusion. This work demonstrates that the configuration of fingers, or hand articulation, offers significant cues for recovering the object's geometry. We introduce a novel approach that leverages hand articulation to infer the object's 3D shape. Our method employs a specialized network to predict 3D object points from the input image, which are then transformed into object space using a hand-object model. A differentiable version of this model facilitates the estimation of pose and size. We further utilize a specialized loss function to align the predicted points with the hand's surface, thereby refining the shape reconstruction. Experiments on the 3D2DS+ dataset confirm that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a new method for deriving sunspot umbral brightness from Ca-K line observations, termed "Equal Contrast" (EC). The EC technique adjusts the background continuum level of Ca-K images to ensure a consistent brightness ratio between the photosphere and sunspot umbra, thereby standardizing the umbral brightness across varying continuum intensities. By applying this method to a dataset of 1,000 Ca-K line images collected by the Heliospheric Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we compared the derived umbbral brightness with that from a 10-year dataset of the same period. The results indicate that the EC-derived umbbral brightness correlates significantly better with spot-free periods than the traditional method, which relies on the original background intensity. Furthermore, we compared the EC-derived umbbral brightness with that obtained from the Heliospheric Imager's extreme ultraviolet (EUV) channel, which is sensitive to the same spectral lines. The findings demonstrate a strong correlation between the EC-derived umbbral brightness and the EUV channel data, suggesting that the EC technique effectively captures the intrinsic physical properties of sunspot umbrae.

Distributed symbolic execution (SE) is a technique for exploring the state space of a program by distributing the work across multiple machines. However, existing methods often fail to utilize the specific nature of the testing task, which aims to cover as many test cases as possible. This paper introduces a new approach called "test-depth partitioning," which assigns testing tasks to machines based on the depth of the states being explored. We demonstrate that this strategy significantly outperforms current methods by reducing the execution time for test case discovery by 20% to 70%, while simultaneously increasing the total number of tests executed by 20% to 50%.

This study examines the magnetization dynamics of an ensemble of interacting magnetic nanoparticles using a kinetic approach. The analysis focuses on how the aspect ratio of the particles influences their relaxation behavior, specifically under varying dipolar interaction strengths. To achieve this, we have developed a kinetic framework that incorporates both the thermal fluctuations of the magnetic moments and the interparticle interactions. The model's predictions are benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data. The results demonstrate that the aspect ratio is a critical parameter for accurately describing the magnetization relaxation of nanoparticle ensembles. Furthermore, we have derived an analytical expression for the magnetization relaxation time, which aligns well with experimental findings.

Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning approach designed for training models across decentralized data sources, making it ideal for privacy-sensitive scenarios. However, FL faces significant challenges when the data across participating nodes is non-IID, as this heterogeneity can lead to suboptimal performance. To address this, we introduce a new framework called FedAvg+, which combines the FedAvg algorithm with a regularization technique to enhance model robustness. Our approach leverages the inherent sparsity of neural network weights to regularize local models, thereby improving their generalization capabilities. We demonstrate that FedAvg+ achieves superior results compared to standard FedAvg, particularly in non-IID settings. Furthermore, we validate our findings through experiments on both synthetic data and real-world datasets.

Short-text classification is a prevalent challenge in natural language processing, with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) being a popular choice for handling sequential data. However, RNNs are often criticized for their slow training and inference speeds, stemming from the necessity of processing data strictly in order. This paper introduces a new approach to classify short texts by leveraging the sequence modeling capabilities of RNNs without adhering to sequential data dependencies. Our method involves training a model on text segments that have been randomly shuffled, thereby eliminating the need for ordered input during inference. Experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that this approach achieves performance comparable to leading short-text classification methods.

This study examines the sensitivity of the electric field in Fabry-P\'{e}rot etalons regarding optical thickness variations, aiming to evaluate the linear response of the system. We derive the sensitivity metric for the amplitude of the electric field and determine its maximum value. The analysis indicates that sensitivity depends on the ratio between the amplitude of the input wave and that reflected from the internal interface. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between sensitivity and the input field's amplitude, as well as the input and output field phases.

A matching is defined as compatible between two labeled convex sets, each containing $n$ vertices, when every edge connects a vertex from the first set to a vertex from the second such that their relative ordering remains invariant. We demonstrate that the maximum number of edges possible in any single compatible matching is bounded by $O(n^{2/3})$. Furthermore, we establish an asymptotically tight lower bound for this result and provide the exact value for cases where $n$ is a power of 2.

The chiplet approach offers a solution to the challenges of integrating multiple vendor-produced dies within a single chip by utilizing standardized interfaces. This work introduces a new methodology for automatically generating these interface specifications, leveraging the observation that such interfaces are fundamentally composed of distinct, well-defined sub-protocols. By utilizing a rule-based system to govern the extraction of these sub-protocols, we demonstrate the ability to automatically derive comprehensive chiplet interfaces from existing protocols. This technique was successfully applied to create standard interfaces for memory controllers and network interfaces, which were then validated through a comprehensive suite of tests.

Mixture cure models are designed to address the issue of cured patients in survival data. This study introduces a Bayesian nonparametric approach for fitting multivariate survival models with a cure rate, grounded in the Dirichlet process prior. This methodology offers significant flexibility, allowing for the modeling of complex multivariate survival distributions. Furthermore, the model incorporates a cure rate parameter within a nonparametric regression framework, enabling the modeling of various cure rate patterns. This approach is extended to handle right-censored data, and the resulting algorithms are derived using the Gibbs sampler. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method yields robust performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph, denoted as $ \text{nd}(G) $, is defined as the cardinality of a nonlocal metric basis $ B $. A vertex set $ B $ qualifies as a nonlocal metric basis if it is minimal such that no vertex outside $ B $ is a nonlocal common neighbor of all members within $ G $. This study establishes several fundamental properties of nonlocal metric bases and determines the nonlocal metric dimensions for various graph types, including complete, path, cycle, complete bipartite, and line graphs. Furthermore, it characterizes trees and complete graphs based on their nonlocal metric dimensions.

In-memory computing systems are designed to minimize the energy consumption of deep neural networks (DNNs) by executing computations directly within memory, thereby eliminating the energy costs associated with data movement. However, the inherent nonlinearity of the charge-based sensing process in these memory cells introduces inaccuracies that degrade DNN performance. To address this, we introduce a self-distillation-based knowledge distillation framework that leverages the teacher's soft labels to correct anomalies in the energy sensing of memory cells. By employing a teacher network to process the same inputs as the student, the teacher generates a set of soft labels reflecting the probability distribution of its predictions. The student then trains to align its outputs with these soft labels, effectively learning from the teacher's insights. To further enhance robustness against outliers, we propose a self-distillation approach that utilizes the soft labels from the student's own previous predictions. Experimental results across various datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 3.4% over existing techniques.

This paper introduces a new class of polar codes termed "short polarization kernels" (SPKs), which are constructed using shortened large polarization kernels (SP-Large Polar Codes). These codes offer superior performance compared to polar codes based on small or medium-sized kernels. Specifically, the SPKs achieve better error correction capabilities than codes derived from small kernels while maintaining the computational efficiency of medium-sized kernel codes. The study details the methodology for generating short large polarization kernels and outlines the specific characteristics of the resulting codes. Furthermore, a software implementation is provided, and simulations confirm that the proposed codes significantly outperform those based on small kernels in terms of performance.

Seismic data denoising is a critical step in processing workflows, and supervised deep learning has emerged as a leading method for this task. However, these models depend on clean reference data for training, which is often unavailable in real-world scenarios. Although recent advancements have introduced unsupervised approaches, they typically rely on the unrealistic assumption that noise is white. This study presents a new unsupervised denoising technique that leverages the inherent sparsity of seismic traces. By applying a sparsity-inducing prior to the noise component, we transform the denoising challenge into a sparse optimization problem. We solve this using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), a technique known for its robustness and efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method effectively removes noise from seismic data and outperforms existing unsupervised techniques.

The JLab experiment E12-06-001 investigates two-photon exchange effects in lepton scattering by utilizing the charge-magnitude difference of the proton's cross sections for electrons and muons. Conducted in 2019 at a beam energy of 11 GeV, this study measured the relative electron-muon cross section ratio at fixed momentum transfer ($Q^2$) for both positive and negative lepton beams, covering a $Q^2$ range from 10 to 20 GeV$^2/c^2$. The resulting data aligns with predictions from the generalized vector-boson model, which accounts for both two-photon and one-photon exchange processes.

The Hubbard model serves as a foundational framework for describing electrons or holes interacting within a lattice, with strong on-site Coulomb repulsion defining the Hubbard model as a basic representation of interacting electrons or holes within a lattice, with strong on-site interactions. In the regime of strong interactions, the system displays a complex interplay between the underlying antiferromagnetic order and the kinetic energy of the charge carriers. This interplay is crucial for understanding high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates, as well as the anomalous properties of transition metal oxides. This review examines the dynamics of strongly interacting electrons and holes in the Hubbard model, specifically focusing on the large-U limit where on-site Coulomb repulsion is maximized. The discussion centers on the low-energy physics of the system, particularly the behavior of "small-polaron" quasiparticles. These are localized entities that arise from the combination of strong electron correlations and the lattice's antiferromagnetic order. The review explores the theoretical foundations of these quasiparticles, including their formation mechanisms, their transport properties, and their role in mediating superconductivity. Furthermore, the text addresses the challenges in understanding the non-perturbative nature of these strongly correlated systems, highlighting the importance of non-perturbative methods in understanding these strongly correlated systems. The review concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the development of new materials with novel electronic properties. Mediation analysis is a fundamental component of causal inference, enabling the quantification of how an independent variable influences a dependent variable through an intermediary mediator. While Bayesian mediation methods are well-documented, they typically depend on custom-written, non-reusable code. To address this, we present MedBayes, an R package designed for flexible and user-friendly Bayesian mediation analysis. The package includes a visual interface for model specification and a `visualize` function that generates plots illustrating the relationships between variables. Furthermore, MedBayes offers several advanced features, such as support for multiple mediators, the ability to handle covariates, and the capacity to incorporate priors. The package is accompanied by a comprehensive user guide and practical examples. The primary objective of MedBayes is to enhance the accessibility of Bayesian mediation techniques for researchers and to foster discussion regarding the application of Bayesian methods in this area. The package is accessible at https://github.com/medbayes/medbayes.
